figures.sourceHeading: Electrolysis cell for collecting gaseous products from aqueous solutions

specPoints.text: describe experiments to investigate electrolysis, using inert electrodes, of molten compounds (including lead(II) bromide) and aqueous solutions (including sodium chloride, dilute sulfuric acid and copper(II) sulfate) and to predict the products
practical: investigate the electrolysis of aqueous solutions

primer.text: From Electrolysis Experiments you know the apparatus and the prediction rules for aqueous electrolysis. This note is the practical itself: electrolyse three named solutions in the lab, collect the gases in inverted test tubes, run the identity tests, and read the products straight off what appears at each electrode.

lessons.title: Method & testing the products
lessons.opening: The experiment electrolyses three solutions, sodium chloride, dilute sulfuric acid and copper(II) sulfate, in a beaker whose electrodes are covered by the liquid. Two inverted test tubes sit over the electrodes to catch any gas, a power pack drives the current, and each collected sample is then tested: a lighted splint for hydrogen, a glowing splint for oxygen, and litmus paper for chlorine.
keyPoints: The aim is to electrolyse sodium chloride, dilute sulfuric acid and copper(II) sulfate solutions, collecting and identifying the products.
The electrodes are covered with the solution, and two inverted test tubes sit over them to collect gases.
The electrodes connect to a power pack or battery, which is switched on to let electrolysis take place.
A gas that burns with a pop from a lighted splint is hydrogen, collected at the cathode.
A gas that relights a glowing splint is oxygen, and a gas that bleaches litmus is chlorine.

low.restatement: Set up the cell with the electrodes covered by the solution and inverted tubes above them, switch on, and watch each electrode. Test any gas with a lighted splint for the pop of hydrogen, a glowing splint for oxygen, or litmus for chlorine, and treat any solid coating as the metal itself.
low.analogy: It is like cooking with a lid: the tubes trap whatever rises, so nothing escapes before you have tasted, or tested, it.
low.examPointer: Name the test for each gas in the right direction: pop means hydrogen at the cathode, relighting means oxygen at the anode, bleaching means chlorine.

medium.restatement: The practical is a controlled comparison: identical apparatus, three different electrolytes, and the same gas tests applied throughout. Inverted tubes accumulate the gaseous products while the current runs, and the testing step names each gas: the cathode pop gives hydrogen, the anode relight gives oxygen, and litmus bleaching gives chlorine.
medium.analogy: Think of three identical kettles boiled with different waters: the apparatus stays constant, so any difference in what collects must come from the liquid, which is the comparison the practical is built on.
medium.examPointer: Solid products count as results too: a pink-brown coat on the cathode of the copper(II) sulfate cell is the copper, and colour is the clue to which metal.

check.stem: Why are two small test tubes inverted over the electrodes?

options.text: To collect the gaseous products so they can be tested
options.explanation: Gases rise into the tubes and accumulate, which is what makes the identification tests possible.

options.text: To keep the solution from evaporating
options.explanation: The tubes sit over the electrodes to trap gas; evaporation is not their purpose.

options.text: To stop the current leaking away
options.explanation: The current flows through the solution between the electrodes; the tubes do not touch the circuit.

options.text: To warm the solution evenly
options.explanation: No heating is intended here; the tubes are collection vessels.

check.stem: Which sequence describes the method correctly?

options.text: Add the solution, cover the electrodes, invert the test tubes, connect the power, then observe and test
options.explanation: The method runs from set-up through powering the cell to the testing step at the end.

options.text: Test the gases first, then start the current
options.explanation: Nothing can be tested before the current has produced it; testing comes last.

options.text: Connect the power before adding any solution
options.explanation: The electrodes must be covered by the solution before the current flows.

options.text: Remove the tubes before switching off the power
options.explanation: The tubes stay in place to collect gas throughout the electrolysis.

check.stem: A gas collected at the cathode burns with a pop when lit. What is it?

options.text: Hydrogen
options.explanation: The pop with a lighted splint is the standard test for hydrogen, collected at the cathode.

options.text: Oxygen
options.explanation: Oxygen is the anode gas and relights a glowing splint rather than popping.

options.text: Chlorine
options.explanation: Chlorine bleaches litmus; it does not burn with a pop.

options.text: Bromine
options.explanation: Bromine has no pop test here; it belongs to molten-compound anodes as brown fumes.

check.stem: A gas collected at the anode relights a glowing splint. What is it?

options.text: Oxygen
options.explanation: Relighting a glowing splint is the classic test for oxygen, which forms at the anode from OH- ions.

options.text: Hydrogen
options.explanation: Hydrogen pops with a lighted splint and forms at the cathode.

options.text: Chlorine
options.explanation: Chlorine bleaches litmus paper; a glowing-splint relight points to oxygen.

options.text: Water vapour
options.explanation: Water vapour neither pops nor relights; the relight is oxygen's signature.

check.stem: What does a solid forming around an electrode tell you?

options.text: That the metal has been formed there, with the colour indicating which metal
options.explanation: Metal deposition shows as a solid coating, and its colour names the metal.

options.text: That the electrode has melted
options.explanation: The electrodes are inert and stay intact; the coating is the product metal.

options.text: That the solution has become saturated
options.explanation: A coating on an electrode is the deposited metal, not crystallised solute.

options.text: That the current has stopped
options.explanation: Deposition happens while the current flows; stopping the current would halt it.

lessons.title: Results & conclusions
lessons.opening: The results table across the three solutions is the practical's payoff. Sodium chloride solution splits into hydrogen at its cathode and chlorine at its anode, the chlorine showing itself by bleaching litmus. Dilute sulfuric acid splits into hydrogen at its cathode and oxygen at its anode, while copper(II) sulfate deposits pink-brown copper at its cathode and gives oxygen at its anode.
keyPoints: Sodium chloride solution splits into hydrogen gas at its cathode and chlorine gas at its anode.
The chlorine at the anode shows itself by bleaching a piece of litmus paper.
Dilute sulfuric acid splits into hydrogen gas at its cathode and oxygen gas at its anode.
Copper(II) sulfate solution yields copper metal at its cathode and oxygen gas at its anode.
The copper appears as a pink-brown deposit on the cathode electrode.

low.restatement: Three solutions, three product pairs: hydrogen and chlorine for sodium chloride, hydrogen and oxygen for dilute sulfuric acid, copper and oxygen for copper(II) sulfate. The gas tests and the pink-brown deposit are the evidence, and the conclusions simply name what each result means.
low.analogy: It is like a tasting menu with three dishes: the same fork and knife do the testing, and each dish announces its own flavour, hydrogen here, chlorine there, copper in the third.
low.examPointer: Quote the results as pairs, cathode and anode together, because the conclusions join the two halves of each row.

medium.restatement: The conclusions follow the prediction rules met earlier: sodium chloride supplies a halide, so chlorine reaches the anode while hydrogen wins the cathode; sulfuric acid offers no halide, so oxygen forms instead; and copper(II) sulfate contributes a metal less reactive than hydrogen, so copper deposits while oxygen forms at the anode.
medium.analogy: Picture three vending machines loaded differently but sharing one mechanism: the mechanism is the rule set, and each machine's stock, the ions in its solution, decides what drops out.
medium.examPointer: Learn the table as three complete rows, cathode and anode together, because exam questions quote one row and expect the missing half.

check.stem: Which products form when sodium chloride solution is electrolysed?

options.text: Hydrogen at the cathode and chlorine at the anode
options.explanation: The solution matches the rules: hydrogen wins the cathode and the halide chlorine reaches the anode.

options.text: Hydrogen at both electrodes
options.explanation: The anode follows the halide rule; chlorine, not hydrogen, forms there.

options.text: Sodium and chlorine
options.explanation: Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so it stays in solution while hydrogen is discharged.

options.text: Oxygen at the anode
options.explanation: Oxygen forms only when no halide is present; chloride ions are present here.

check.stem: What does the sodium chloride anode gas do to litmus paper?

options.text: It bleaches the litmus, identifying the gas as chlorine
options.explanation: Bleaching is chlorine's signature test, recorded in the results table.

options.text: It turns the litmus red permanently
options.explanation: The recorded effect is bleaching, not a permanent red stain.

options.text: Nothing, the paper is unaffected
options.explanation: Chlorine's bleaching action is exactly what the paper shows.

options.text: It dissolves the paper
options.explanation: The gas bleaches the litmus; it does not dissolve it.

check.stem: Which row correctly completes the results table for dilute sulfuric acid?

options.text: Cathode: colourless gas that pops with a lighted splint; anode: colourless gas that relights a glowing splint
options.explanation: The acid gives hydrogen at the cathode and oxygen at the anode, both colourless gases.

options.text: Cathode: gas that pops; anode: gas that bleaches litmus
options.explanation: Bleaching belongs to the sodium chloride row; the acid gives oxygen at the anode.

options.text: Cathode: pink-brown deposit; anode: gas that relights
options.explanation: The pink-brown deposit is the copper(II) sulfate row; the acid gives hydrogen gas at the cathode.

options.text: Cathode: no change; anode: no change
options.explanation: Both electrodes show gas evolution in this cell.

check.stem: What is observed at the cathode when copper(II) sulfate solution is electrolysed?

options.text: A pink-brown deposit of copper on the electrode
options.explanation: Copper is less reactive than hydrogen, so it deposits, and its colour is pink-brown.

options.text: A colourless gas that pops
options.explanation: Hydrogen pops at the cathode only when the metal is more reactive than hydrogen; copper's ion is discharged instead.

options.text: A grey metal coating of zinc
options.explanation: The deposited metal is copper, not zinc; the solution contains copper ions.

options.text: Bubbles of chlorine
options.explanation: Chlorine needs chloride ions, which copper(II) sulfate does not contain.

check.stem: Which conclusion pairs each solution with its two products correctly?

options.text: Sodium chloride: hydrogen and chlorine; sulfuric acid: hydrogen and oxygen; copper(II) sulfate: copper and oxygen
options.explanation: The three conclusions read straight off the results table.

options.text: Sodium chloride: sodium and chlorine; sulfuric acid: hydrogen and oxygen; copper(II) sulfate: copper and oxygen
options.explanation: Sodium is not discharged; hydrogen forms at the cathode of the sodium chloride cell.

options.text: Sodium chloride: hydrogen and oxygen; sulfuric acid: hydrogen and chlorine; copper(II) sulfate: hydrogen and copper
options.explanation: The anode products of the first two rows have been swapped.

options.text: All three give hydrogen at the anode
options.explanation: Hydrogen is a cathode product in every row; the anodes give chlorine or oxygen.

glossary.definition: The splitting of a molten or dissolved compound by an electric current.
The solution being electrolysed, which conducts through its moving ions.
The negatively charged electrode, where hydrogen pops or the metal deposits.
The positively charged electrode, where oxygen or chlorine is released.
Paper indicator used here to detect chlorine, which bleaches it.

workedExample.prompt: Three aqueous solutions — sodium chloride, dilute sulfuric acid and copper(II) sulfate — are electrolysed with inert electrodes and the products are collected. a) The gas at the cathode in the sulfuric acid cell burns with a 'pop'. Identify it. b) The gas at the anode in the sodium chloride cell bleaches litmus. Identify it and name the cathode product of this cell. c) A pink-brown deposit forms on the cathode of the copper(II) sulfate cell. Name the deposit and the anode product.
steps: a) A gas that burns with a 'pop' from a lighted splint is hydrogen, so dilute sulfuric acid gives hydrogen at the cathode (with oxygen at the anode).
b) A gas that bleaches litmus paper is chlorine; the conclusion of record pairs it with hydrogen at the cathode for sodium chloride solution.
c) A pink-brown deposit on an electrode is the metal itself — copper — and the copper(II) sulfate cell gives oxygen at the anode, confirmed by the gas relighting a glowing splint.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) Hydrogen. b) Chlorine at the anode; hydrogen at the cathode. c) Copper at the cathode; oxygen at the anode.
